{"[2018DA1049]": "We consider the grounds for final appeal.

1. Civil Act Article 860 provides in its main text that “인지는 그 자의 출생 시에 소급하여 효력이 생긴다,” while its proviso states that “그러나 제삼자의 취득한 권리를 해하지 못한다,” thereby limiting the retroactive effect of acknowledgment; and Civil Act Article 1014 provides that “상속개시 후의 인지 또는 재판의 확정에 의하여 공동상속인이 된 자가 상속재산의 분할을 청구할 경우에 다른 공동상속인이 이미 분할 기타 처분을 한 때에는 그 상속분에 상당한 가액의 지급을 청구할 권리가 있다.”
However, between a child born out of wedlock and the birth mother, a legal parent-child relationship arises automatically by the child’s birth without waiting for the birth mother’s acknowledgment or birth registration (see Supreme Court Judgment 67DA1791, rendered October 4, 1967), and it is not the case that such relationship may be recognized only where there is an entry in the family relation register or a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship by a court (see Supreme Court Judgment 92NU3199, rendered July 10, 1992). Therefore, the proviso to Civil Act Article 860 concerning the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment does not apply, nor is it applied by analogy, to a mother-child relationship that does not require acknowledgment, and it cannot be said on the basis of Civil Act Article 1014, which prescribes the right of a person who became a co-heir by acknowledgment or by a final and conclusive judgment after the opening of succession to claim payment of value, that such person may not deny the effect of the division or disposition of inherited property made by the mother’s other co-heir. The same applies even if the mother-child relationship was only later made clear through the finality of a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship, etc., after another co-heir had already partitioned or disposed of the inherited property.
2. a. According to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below determined as follows. Inherited property that was partitioned or disposed of by co-heirs before acknowledgment definitively vests in the co-heir who received the partition or the transferee, pursuant to the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment prescribed in the proviso to Civil Act Article 860, and this legal principle also applies where a person who was later determined to be an heir by the finality of an action for confirmation of the existence of a parent-child relationship after the opening of succession comes into existence. The judgment that a biological parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiff (selected party) and the designated parties (hereinafter referred to as “the Plaintiffs, etc.”) and Non-party 1 became final after Defendant 1 disposed of the real property listed in Attached List 1 of the judgment below (hereinafter referred to as “the Real Property”) to Defendant 2 and completed the registration of transfer of ownership. Ultimately, the Plaintiffs, etc. fall under “a person who became a co-heir by the finality of a judgment after the opening of succession” under Civil Act Article 1014, and therefore may exercise only the right to claim payment of value equivalent to the purchase price against Defendant 1, and may not deny the effect of the disposition of the Real Property, whose ownership was definitively vested in Defendant 2.
b. However, the above determination by the court below is difficult to accept as it stands for the following reasons.
1) According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.
a) Non-party 1 married Non-party 2 and gave birth to Defendant 1, and thereafter divorced, while maintaining a de facto marital relationship with Non-party 3 and giving birth to the Plaintiffs, etc.
b) Non-party 1 owned the Real Property and died on January 27, 2015. After Defendant 1 completed the registration of transfer of ownership on the Real Property on the grounds of inheritance on June 8, 2015, Defendant 1 sold the Real Property to Defendant 2 on June 25, 2015 and completed the registration of transfer of ownership around that time.
c) On February 12, 2016, the Plaintiffs, etc. filed an action seeking confirmation that a biological parent-child relationship existed between Non-party 1 and the Plaintiffs, etc., and on July 1, 2016, the judgment granting that claim became final and conclusive.
2) In light of the foregoing legal principle, the facts above indicate that between the Plaintiffs, etc. and their birth mother, Non-party 1, a legal parent-child relationship arose automatically by the birth of the Plaintiffs, etc., and it is not the case that such relationship may be recognized only if there is a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship by a court.
Therefore, the proviso to Civil Act Article 860 does not apply, nor is it applied by analogy, between the Plaintiffs, etc. and Non-party 1, and it cannot be said on the basis of Civil Act Article 1014 that the Plaintiffs, etc. may not deny the effect of Defendant 1’s disposition of the Real Property. The same applies even if the judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship between the Plaintiffs, etc. and Non-party 1 became final and conclusive only after Defendant 1 had already disposed of the Real Property, thereby making the mother-child relationship clear only then.
c. Nevertheless, the court below, on the grounds set forth above, dismissed the Plaintiffs, etc.’s claim seeking cancellation of the registration of transfer of co-ownership shares in the names of the Defendants with respect to the Real Property, thereby committing an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the mother-child relationship and the scope of application of the proviso to Civil Act Article 860 and Article 1014. The allegation in the grounds of final appeal pointing this out has merit.
3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds for final appeal, the part of the judgment below against the Plaintiffs, etc. is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination. It is so decided by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision.

{"[2020SEU616]": "We decide the grounds for the re-appeal.

1. Overview of the Case and Issue
A. Overview of the Case
The applicant and the person concerned in this case, male로 출생한 신청인(이하 'Applicant')은 childhood부터 여성으로의 귀속감을 가졌고, puberty에 이르러 얼굴 형태, 체격, 목소리가 점점 남성적으로 변하는 것에 정신적 고통을 겪었지만 자신의 성정체성을 숨긴 채 생활하다가 혼인하였고, 성정체성 문제로 혼인한 지 약 5년 10개월 만에 이혼하였다. Thereafter, around 2018. 11., the Applicant underwent surgery at a plastic surgery clinic in Thailand to remove the testicles and penis and to form the appearance of female external genitalia, and has since lived socially as a woman, wearing women’s clothes and hairstyle. While having 2 minor children, twins born in 2012, the Applicant filed an application for permission to correct the gender entry in the Family Relations Register, that is, the permission application in this case.
The court below upheld the first-instance decision dismissing the permission application on the ground that, because the Applicant has minor children, permitting correction of the gender entry would have a negative effect on the welfare of the minor children.

B. Issue in this Case
The Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009스117 held that, in granting permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, if the person is presently married or has minor children, correction of the gender entry is not permitted. The issue in this case is limited to the latter, namely whether it is appropriate to regard the existence of minor children in the case of a transsexual person who is not presently married as an independent negative requirement for correction of the gender entry.

2. Determination of the Sex of a Transsexual Person and Correction of the Gender Entry in the Family Relations Register
A. The factors determining a person’s sex include not only biological factors such as sex chromosomes and the genitalia corresponding thereto, but also 정신적 and social factors, such as the individual’s own sense of belonging to the male or female sex and the performance of sex roles, that is, socially approved behavior, attitude, and personality traits appropriate for a male or female.
In the case of a person with transsexualism, during the growth process after birth, such person consistently has a sense of incongruity, discomfort, and aversion toward the biological sex at birth and feels a sense of belonging to a different sex, while continuously and firmly performing roles appropriate to the sex with which he or she feels a sense of belonging, so that mental and social adaptation has been achieved as a sex different from the sex at birth. Further, if such person can be recognized, by ordinary medical standards, as not easily being assessed as the sex at birth, and has reached the degree of recognition and acceptance as the transitioned sex in physical appearance such as genitalia, clothing, and hairstyle, as well as in personal domains such as sexual relations and friendships and social domains such as occupation, and thus can be deemed, even from a social-normative perspective, to have the transitioned sex, then such a transsexual person may be legally evaluated as having the transitioned sex, not the sex at birth.

B. The Supreme Court, in its En Banc Decision dated June 22, 2006, 2004스42, held, on the basis of the foregoing legal principles, that with respect to an application for permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, in the case of a transsexual person the sex at birth and the sex legally evaluated at present are different, and therefore the entry of sex in the family register, which can now be regarded as corresponding to the Family Relations Register under the current Family Relations Registration Act, would fail to publicly disclose the current true status relationship, so the sex legally evaluated at present must be reflected in the family register, and accordingly permitted correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person. Furthermore, because such permission for correction of the gender entry is a decision intended to confirm the current true sex newly legally evaluated according to transsexuality, it was held that the effect of the decision granting permission for correction of the family register or the correction of the gender entry based thereon does not affect the existing status relationship and rights and obligations.
However, the Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009스117 held that, if a transsexual person has minor children, the welfare of the minor children must be considered first, and that the correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children is not permitted, on the grounds that correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register may cause mental confusion and shock to the minor children, and that disclosure of the family relations certificate may expose the minor children to social discrimination and prejudice or cause difficulties in daily life.

3. Whether Permission for Correction of the Gender Entry of a Transsexual Person with Minor Children Should Be Granted and the Standard for Such Determination
Every human being has the right to form a personality according to his or her gender identity and to live his or her life. A transsexual person also should be able to realize personality and individuality based on his or her gender identity and live together with others as an equal member of our society while pursuing happiness. In order to fully exercise such rights, a transsexual person has the right to have his or her sex according to his or her gender identity legally confirmed as the true sex. This is a fundamental right derived from human dignity and value, and forms the essence of the right to pursue happiness; therefore, it must be guaranteed to the fullest extent.
Meanwhile, a transsexual person with minor children also has the duty, as a parent, to protect and educate the children, and must prioritize the welfare of the children even when exercising parental authority. Therefore, when determining whether to grant permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children, the court must make a substantive determination by comprehensively considering various circumstances for the balance of legal interests so as to harmonize protection of the transsexual person’s fundamental rights with the protection and welfare of the minor children. Accordingly, one must not refuse correction of the gender entry merely on the ground that the transsexual person has minor children, without making a substantive determination in light of the above circumstances. The reasons are as follows.

A. Regarding Whether to Grant Permission for Correction of the Gender Entry of a Transsexual Person with Minor Children
1) Protection of Fundamental Rights Such as Human Dignity and Value, and the Right to Pursue Happiness of a Transsexual Person
(a) All citizens have dignity and value as human beings, have the right to pursue happiness, and shall be equal before the law. Human dignity and value imply that each individual should be respected for his or her unique personality and individuality, and should be able freely to choose and develop the content and direction of life deemed most suitable, thereby forming the self and destiny. A transsexual person, too, as an equal member of our society, has dignity and value as a human being, the right to pursue happiness, and the right to live a life worthy of a human being, and these rights must be protected. Therefore, even when determining whether to grant permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, such fundamental rights of the transsexual person as a human being must be guaranteed to the fullest extent.
(b) Considering the role that the distinction and recognition of sex plays in society, it is ultimately consistent with maintaining order in society as a whole and with the public welfare to ensure that an individual’s actual sex and the sex publicly disclosed do not conflict by having the individual publicly confirm and disclose his or her sex in a manner consistent with the sex currently legally evaluated. That a transsexual person publicly obtains legal sex in accordance with his or her gender identity through correction of the gender entry does not in itself have any potential to directly harm other members of society. Rather, if the true sex confirmed according to an individual’s gender identity exists, but the sex publicly disclosed through the Family Relations Register does not correspond to it, and that situation is left uncorrected, there is a high likelihood that confusion and misunderstanding will arise among other members of society as a result.
(c) It is correct to view the confirmation of sex in both private and public spheres as an essential condition of life for maintaining human dignity, which is determined prior to a person’s position or role within the family order. If permission for correction of the gender entry were denied merely because a transsexual person has minor children, then, contrary to the appearance and actual life formed in accordance with his or her gender identity, the person would be displayed in the official records as the sex before transition, and would be compelled to live an absurd life in which the sex as actually existing and the sex as shown in official records are inconsistent. If such an absurd situation is forced upon the person for a long period until the minor children reach adulthood, the magnitude of the suffering that the transsexual person must endure personally and socially, and the urgency of confronting absurdity in order to exist, would inevitably become immense. Such a result infringes the essential content of the constitutional demand to respect human dignity and value and to guarantee the right not to be discriminated against on the basis of gender identity, and is thus unacceptable.
(d) An individual’s family life forms the beginning and core of social relationships, and the State must guarantee it. A transsexual person, too, as a member who forms a family within the overall legal order, should be granted equal rights and duties, and the State must protect such rights of the transsexual person.
Although granting permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children may bring about changes in family relations, this is nothing more than a natural process in which the manner in which the rights and duties of the parent are realized changes accordingly as the fact of one parent’s transsexuality occurs. The parent-child relationship and family order thus formed must also be equally respected and protected within the overall legal order. This does not change merely because the transsexual person is divorced and not presently married, or because correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register has been made. A transsexual person with minor children must still exercise the rights and perform the duties that accompany his or her role as father or mother, and is able to do so.

2) Welfare of Minor Children
(a) It is not correct to uniformly conclude that granting permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children by itself causes a major change in the status relationship between the person exercising parental authority and the minor children, or is manifestly contrary to the welfare of the children, or leaves minor children exposed without protection to social prejudice and discrimination.
(b) Correction of the gender entry merely accepts the actual situation of a transsexual person who has completed transition and reflects it in the official record; it does not newly cause major changes in the status relationship between the transsexual parent and the minor children, or affect the substance of rights and obligations. This is because the personal, social, and legal parent-child relationship between a transsexual person and his or her minor children does not change regardless of whether it is before or after correction of the gender entry. Nor can the correction of the gender entry itself be regarded as impairing the essential and core content of the transsexual person’s status and role as father or mother within the family system, or the rights of the minor children.
(c) Even if minor children in some cases suffer mental confusion and shock due to a parent’s transsexuality, such confusion and shock arise because the parent has already undergone the transition, making it an irreversible fait accompli. Correction of the gender entry is a measure that corrects the sex entry in the official record so that a person who has already transitioned in social common sense can be legally evaluated as having the transitioned sex. Therefore, one must not hastily conclude that the permission itself for correction of the gender entry, which can be said to be the final stage of the transition process, causes mental or psychological shock to the minor children.
Likewise, the premise that adult children can accept a parent’s correction of the gender entry without much confusion, whereas minor children will suffer mental confusion and shock, is also incorrect. This overlooks the possibility that minor children, with their flexible minds, may naturally accept the existence of a transsexual parent.
(d) If an emotional and familial bond has already formed between the transsexual person and the minor children based on the transitioned sex of the father or mother, then it is desirable to grant permission for correction of the gender entry even for the sake of the minor children.
Furthermore, even in cases where the minor children have not yet adapted psychologically to the transitioned sex of the father or mother and are suffering psychological and emotional difficulties, if a divorced transsexual father or mother, through correction of the gender entry, provides a social and economic foundation enabling him or her to continue stably raising and supporting the minor children as a parent and an opportunity to seek understanding of transsexuality, this can ultimately serve the welfare of the minor children in that it may restore the bond between them. This is because a transsexual person whose actual sex conflicts with the sex publicly disclosed in the Family Relations Register may in some cases find it difficult in society to choose a job suited to appearance or to engage in economic and social activities corresponding to ability and aptitude, and the minor children of such a transsexual person are likely, while observing such father or mother, to become emotionally more unstable and to face the risk of being placed in a financially poorer environment.
Therefore, without examining the various situations existing or arising between the transitioned father or mother and the minor children, the court may, in a substantive sense, fail to act in accordance with the welfare of the minor children by barring correction of the gender entry merely on the ground that there are minor children.
(e) It cannot be concluded that, if permission for correction of the gender entry is granted to a transsexual person with minor children, the minor children will be left exposed without protection to social discrimination and prejudice or placed in difficulties in daily life merely because of the submission or disclosure of the corrected Family Relations Register.
Even if there is a concern that disclosure of the Family Relations Register may expose the minor children to social prejudice and discrimination, the State should protect the minor children by taking measures to block such disclosure for the purpose of safeguarding the fundamental rights and privacy of transsexual persons and their minor children; it is not proper to use that concern as a reason for refusing permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children.
(1) Our society has for quite some time now recognized transsexual persons, regardless of whether correction of the gender entry is granted, by assessing a person’s sex normatively according to individual and social recognition, and not merely the biological sex at birth. In reality, transsexual persons are a minority in our society, but as neighbors they live ordinary daily lives like everyone else, and many of them increasingly communicate actively by revealing the forms of their lives through the mass media and the like. Although the level of average understanding of transsexual persons in our society has increased, it is also true that discrimination against and exclusion of transsexual persons still exist in our society. As a result, if the fact that the sex of a transsexual father or mother has been corrected is disclosed to the outside through the Family Relations Register, de facto discrimination may arise for the minor children. However, such a problem can be solved by the State’s improving the contents and procedures of the Family Relations Register system and taking measures to prevent the fact of a transsexual person’s correction of the gender entry from being disclosed, thereby protecting the privacy of transsexual persons and their minor children.
Also, in light of the spirit of our Constitution, which places human dignity as its ultimate goal, the State bears the duty to be careful that acts unlawfully exposing matters related to correction of the gender entry in an individual’s Family Relations Register to the outside do not occur, and to make legal and institutional efforts to correct prejudice and misunderstanding on the part of those who discriminate against transsexual persons or their families; yet refusing permission for correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register of a transsexual person on the above grounds is difficult to accept, because it abandons the State’s fundamental duty to prevent harm that transsexual persons and their minor children may suffer from social prejudice and to guarantee the stability of family life.
(2) The Personal Information Protection Act was enacted on March 29, 2011 and came into force on September 30, 2011 in order to promote the rights and interests of citizens and realize individual dignity and value, and the Family Relations Registration Act has also improved the problem that personal information was easily disclosed for the protection of individual privacy.
The current Family Relations Registration Act, in principle, allows certificates containing only essential information for each type of certificate to be used, allows the applicant to obtain a certificate by selecting only the information necessary for the purpose of use, or restricts the persons entitled to request issuance of a certificate, and newly introduced certificates in the form of partial certificates showing only some recorded items. Meanwhile, a person requesting submission of a certificate must request a certificate containing only the minimum family relation registration information necessary for the purpose of use, and use of a submitted certificate for purposes other than the purpose of use is prohibited.
Under the Family Relations Registration Act, only the person concerned, his or her spouse, parents, or children may inspect the Family Relations Register; only the person concerned, his or her spouse, or lineal blood relatives may obtain certificates under the Family Relations Registration Act; and in the case of obtaining a family relation certificate for a minor child, either the father or the mother may be selected, and a family relation certificate, specific certificate, certifying the parent-child relationship only between that parent and the child may be issued.
Also, due to the enforcement of the Electronic Government Act, schools, administrative agencies, and public institutions, unless special circumstances exist, process matters that can prove family relations after verifying them in an information system available within the scope of the relevant duties without requiring submission or presentation by the party.
(3) In light of the current statutory provisions and the social reality concerning the operation of the system as described above, the possibility that, at the stages of inspection, issuance, and submission of a family relation certificate for a minor child, the fact that the minor child’s father or mother has had the gender entry corrected will be carelessly disclosed to a third party is low.

3) Current Status of International Norms and Global Trends Regarding Correction of the Gender Entry of a Transsexual Person
Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides: 'Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this Declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status.' On July 15, 2016, the United Nations Human Rights Council reaffirmed that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights and are entitled to the freedoms and rights set forth in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and adopted a resolution opposing violence and discrimination worldwide based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and our country, as a member state, voted in favor of that resolution.
Also, the majority of countries in the world, including Germany, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Sweden, and the United States, permit correction of the gender entry for transsexual persons, and most countries except Japan do not treat the fact that a transsexual person has minor children as an absolute reason for denying correction of the gender entry. Therefore, refusing to permit correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person merely because the person has minor children runs counter to international human rights norms that all human beings, including transsexual persons, have dignity and rights as human beings and are entitled to enjoy them, and does not conform to the attitudes of countries around the world or the demands of the times.

B. Standard for Determining Whether Permission for Correction of the Gender Entry Should Be Granted
1) When determining whether to grant permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children, the constitutional fundamental rights of the transsexual person himself or herself, such as human dignity and value, the right to pursue happiness, and the right to equality, must be guaranteed to the fullest extent, while at the same time the welfare of the child, including the child’s right to receive protection and care, must be kept in mind. Therefore, in such cases, in addition to whether the general requirements for permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person have been satisfied, the court must examine, by considering all circumstances such as the age and physical and mental condition of the minor children, the degree of the minor children’s consent to or understanding of the father’s or mother’s correction of the gender entry, the form of protection and upbringing of the minor children, the manner in which the transsexual person performs his or her role as father or mother, the relationship and bond the transsexual person has formed and maintained with the minor children and other family members, and other family circumstances, whether granting permission for correction of the gender entry of the transsexual person affects the welfare of the minor children, and determine whether to grant such permission.
2) In individual and concrete cases, the court must, according to such standards, closely examine the actual emotional, economic, and social circumstances experienced by the transitioned father or mother and the minor children, and make a substantive determination as to which decision protects the transsexual person’s fundamental human rights while also conforming to the welfare of the minor children, whether the disadvantages suffered by the minor children from granting permission for correction of the gender entry are markedly greater and more serious than restricting or infringing the transsexual person’s rights based on human dignity under the Constitution, and whether, despite the existence of alternatives that could reduce the disadvantages to the minor children, refusing permission for correction of the gender entry of the father or mother until the minor children reach adulthood and thereby forcing the transsexual person’s suffering arising from the mismatch between actual sex and the sex shown in the official record is consistent with the principle of proportionality. Without doing so, to treat the transsexual person’s correction of the gender entry as contrary to the welfare of the minor children based on vague and abstract concerns and uniformly and completely deny it may, in light of the balance among legal interests, not only infringe the transsexual person’s constitutional fundamental rights but also produce a result that undermines the substantive welfare of the minor children.

4. Change of Precedent
Therefore, the Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009스117, which held to the effect that correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register of a transsexual person is not permitted when the transsexual person has minor children, as well as decisions to the same effect, are all to be changed to the extent they are contrary to the view of this decision.

5. Determination in this Case
We examine the reasoning of the court below’s decision in light of the legal principles seen above. The court below cited the Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009스117, and, viewing the existence of minor children as an independent negative requirement for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, refused the permission application in this case merely on the ground that the Applicant has minor children, without specifically examining the various circumstances appearing in the record of this case and making a substantive determination. In the court below’s determination, there is a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the constitutional fundamental rights under the Constitution’s Preamble to Article 10 that all citizens have dignity and value as human beings and the right to pursue happiness, Article 11(1) that all citizens are equal before the law, and the criteria for granting permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, and there is also an error affecting the judgment by failing to conduct the necessary trial. The Applicant’s assertion of the grounds for re-appeal pointing out this error is well-founded.

6. Conclusion
Therefore, we reverse the court below’s decision and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and so decide as stated in the order. Except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Dong-won, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are supplementary opinions to the majority opinion by Justice Park Jung-hwa, Justice Noh Jeong-hee, and Justice Lee Heung-gu, as well as supplementary opinions by Justice Kim Seon-su and Justice Oh Kyung-mi.

7. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Dong-won
Justice Lee Dong-won’s dissenting opinion is as follows.
A. The previously existing Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009스117, held that, if a transsexual person has minor children, correction of the gender entry is not permitted. As grounds, it stated that under our Civil Act system, in legally evaluating the sex of a person exercising parental authority, the welfare of the minor children must be considered first, and that if such permission were allowed, the special status relationship between the person exercising parental authority and the minor children and the negative impact on the welfare of the minor children would be significant.
The majority opinion appears to view the Supreme Court’s Second En Banc Decision as newly establishing the fact that a transsexual person has minor children as an independent negative requirement for permission to correct the gender entry. However, even before the Second En Banc Decision, the Supreme Court had already, in its En Banc Decision dated June 22, 2006, 2004스42, presented the basic principle that, in order to permit correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, 'it must not cause a significant change in the status relationship with others or have a negative impact on society, and therefore must be socially acceptable.' The Second En Banc Decision merely clarified that the case of a transsexual person with minor children falls within a case contrary to such basic principle; it did not newly establish an independent negative requirement for permission to correct the gender entry.
Because the Second En Banc Decision is consistent with our legal system and the welfare of minor children, and is also a rational decision conforming to the general common sense of society, it should be maintained as is. I cannot agree with the majority opinion attempting to change it. Below, I will examine the reasons in detail.
B. Article 36(1) of the Constitution provides: 'Marriage and family life shall be founded and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and the equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this.' This shows that our Constitution presupposes that the marriage and family system, the most basic unit of our society and the foundation of common life in all spheres, is founded and maintained through the union of differentiated sexes on the premise of the distinction between the sexes. In addition, the Constitution contains various provisions dividing men and women and requiring special protection of women within a certain range, and especially in the field of the marriage and family system, it requires the State to strive to protect women, that is, maternity, which is directly related to pregnancy and childbirth of children.
Considering the text of the Constitution and the Civil Act and the history and structure of enactment and amendment thereof, it is clear that our legal system, including the Constitution and Civil Act, presupposes that a father is a male and a mother is a female. Therefore, under our Constitution, Civil Act, and other statutes, a female father or male mother cannot be permitted. Accordingly, granting permission for correction of the gender entry to a transsexual person who has children would amount to creating a parent-child relationship not permitted under our legal system. By contrast, because our statutes do not distinguish between male and female with respect to the sex of children, even if correction of the gender entry is permitted for a transsexual child, the parent-child relationship does not deviate from our legal system. The argument that, because correction of the gender entry of a transsexual child is possible, correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person who has children must also be possible is based on a failure to properly see the essence of the issue.
However, according to the Second En Banc Decision, if a transsexual person has minor children, correction of the gender entry is not permitted, whereas if a transsexual person has adult children, the conclusion is that correction of the gender entry may be permitted if, by comprehensively considering various circumstances, it is recognized that the person has the transitioned sex physically in social common sense; and it is true that this aspect is not consistent with the above legal system. Although it is not legally consistent to distinguish between cases where there are adult children and cases where there are minor children and to treat the permissibility of correction of the gender entry differently, this can be understood in that it was done by weighing the systematic conformity of our legal system and legal stability against the need for correction of the gender entry, considering that if the same legal logic were adhered to and correction of the gender entry were not permitted even when the transsexual person has adult children, the rights of the transsexual person would be excessively restricted.
C. In the First En Banc Decision, the Supreme Court took the position that correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person cannot be permitted in cases 'where it causes a significant change in the status relationship with others or has a negative impact on society,' and in the Second En Banc Decision, 'where a transsexual person has minor children' was given as a representative example. This stems from the fact that, from the transsexual person’s perspective, if correction of the gender entry is permitted, the person gains the benefit of full protection of constitutional fundamental rights, whereas from the perspective of the minor children in a parent-child relationship with the transsexual person, the status relationship or welfare is bound to be seriously adversely affected, and there is no legal basis sufficient to justify the disadvantages the children would suffer in such a case.
Where a person with issues of sexual identity marries of his or her own choice and has children, or, even without marrying, has children, this is because the person has consented to accept the sex at birth and has decided to form family relations and carried that out; therefore, if the person changes sex at that stage, this cannot be viewed merely as a matter at the personal level. This is because a significant impact is caused to the status relationship or rights of others who formed family relations with that person. The issue of transsexuality at such a stage should be viewed as a matter of change of sex, not correction of the gender entry.
D. Our Civil Act provides that parents become the persons exercising parental authority over their minor children, that a person exercising parental authority has the right and duty to protect and educate the child, and that in exercising parental authority, the welfare of the child must be considered first. Although parental authority is provided in the form of a right in the statutory text, by its nature it has both the character of a right and the character of a duty, and in particular in modern times its aspect as a duty is more emphasized. Therefore, a person exercising parental authority must exercise it in a manner consistent with the 'welfare of the child,' and in some cases must also endure restrictions on the fundamental rights of the individual person exercising parental authority for the 'welfare of the child.'
Such an interpretation is also consistent with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which declares the principle of the 'best interests of the child'. Furthermore, in light of our society’s view of family, which particularly values bonds and consideration among family members, expecting a person exercising parental authority to refrain as much as possible from entering into the series of processes for transsexual transition and correction of the gender entry for the welfare of the child, and even if not possible, to maintain a more cautious and sincere attitude in deciding each step, is the minimum request for consideration that current our society can make of a person who, of his or her own choice, married the opposite sex, gave birth to children, and formed a family.

E. Even if, as the majority opinion states, one were to take the position that the Court must determine whether permission for correction of the gender entry of the Applicant would specifically and seriously affect the minor children and significantly contradict their welfare before deciding whether to grant permission, in this case, considering the following circumstances in combination, the Applicant’s correction of the gender entry cannot be permitted, and therefore the court below’s decision must be maintained as is.
1) The Applicant formed a parent-child relationship with the children by giving birth to them through sexual relations with the opposite sex by the Applicant’s own choice. In such a situation, it does not seem excessive to require the Applicant to place the welfare of the minor children first.
2) In this case, the Applicant has concealed from the children the fact that the Applicant is their father and is pretending to be an aunt. Such a situation cannot be regarded as a case where a natural family relationship has formed according to the transitioned sex of the parent. Nevertheless, if the Applicant’s correction of the gender entry is hastily permitted, there is ample room to regard that as contrary to the welfare of the child.
3) There may be an argument that, since the Applicant is concealing his or her status from the children by pretending to be an aunt, and correction of the gender entry would merely change the sex of the Applicant who had been pretending to be an aunt, there would be no additional mental confusion or shock for the minor children. Such an argument is possible only when the issue of a transsexual person’s correction of the gender entry is viewed solely as an issue after the point at which the sex is corrected and entered in the Family Relations Register. The court must not merely measure fragmentary advantages or disadvantages after a certain point, but must seriously and cautiously consider what decision is best for the welfare of the child by comprehensively examining all circumstances anticipated throughout the process before and after.
4) In ordinary cases, the mental shock or confusion of minor children is more likely to arise not during the correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register concerning a transsexual person, but from the actual change in the physical appearance of the father or mother that occurs beforehand. However, in this case, the minor children knew the Applicant as an aunt rather than as a father, and thus did not experience the Applicant’s physical appearance change. Rather, they are very likely to experience mental shock or confusion later in the process of inspecting or obtaining the family relation certificate and thereby becoming aware of it.
There may be an argument that if minor children suffer mental shock, it can be addressed through psychological counseling or treatment. However, that is not a position that a court, which must interpret and apply the law by prioritizing the welfare of minor children whose ability to adapt has not matured and whose sensitivity is acute, should adopt.
F. In light of the above legal principles and factual circumstances, the court below’s action in upholding the first-instance decision dismissing the Applicant’s application for correction of the gender entry, where the Applicant has minor children, is proper, and there is no error such as that alleged as grounds for the re-appeal. Therefore, the re-appeal should be dismissed.

8. Supplementary Opinion to the Majority Opinion by Justice Park Jung-hwa, Justice Noh Jeong-hee, and Justice Lee Heung-gu
While supplementing the majority opinion, I wish to rebut, to the extent necessary, some of the arguments presented in the dissenting opinion.
The dissenting opinion says that the Second En Banc Decision should be maintained because it is a rational decision consistent with our legal system, the welfare of minor children, and the general common sense of society. However, such dissenting opinion is difficult to accept because it is contrary to the purpose of the First En Banc Decision, infringes the essential content of the transsexual person’s fundamental rights, and may also run counter to the welfare of minor children. The reasons are as follows.
A. Gender identity refers to the internal and personal experience and deep sense of belonging that a human being feels with respect to gender, irrespective of the sex assigned at birth. Every human being, through gender identity in society, recognizes the self and completes a personal narrative by reinterpreting and reconstructing personal experiences and giving them meaning. The right concerning gender identity is one of the principal contents of the general personality right derived from the Constitution, and has significant meaning in the very existence of the individual or the mode of life.
A transsexual person refers to a person whose manifestation of gender identity differs from the biological sex possessed at birth. Human society has divided human beings into male or female based on biological sex at birth and regarded this as an unchangeable absolute, and by recognizing transsexual persons as a third existence that is neither male nor female, or by denying the very existence of those who do clearly exist in actual society, has religiously and socially forced transsexual persons to abandon or conceal their own gender identity. However, it has long been medically, scientifically, and philosophically verified that transsexual persons are also one form of human existence. The State has a duty to uphold the rights concerning gender identity of transsexual persons guaranteed by the Constitution, even in order to overcome this reality.
B. All citizens have the right to have the sex corresponding to their gender identity indicated consistently in the official record. This right has particular significance for transsexual persons. Because a transsexual person who has acquired a gender identity different from the biological sex at birth is publicly recorded in the Family Relations Register according to biological classification, such a person inevitably faces serious problems arising from inconsistency between reality and public record during the process of transition. If the State does not guarantee a procedural right to correct the official record so that it accords with their true gender identity, this infringes the essential content of the transsexual person’s right concerning gender identity.
C. When fundamental rights or public interests and other legal interests conflict, the issue must be resolved according to the principle of practical concordance of legal interests. Because restricting the right of a transsexual person to correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register constitutes an infringement of the essential content of the transsexual person’s human dignity and value and the right to pursue happiness, and the degree of restriction of fundamental rights is very large and serious, there must be serious and clear circumstances showing the necessity to protect or realize other legal interests or values through such restriction, and that there is no alternative other than such restriction. In other words, the right of a transsexual person to correction of the gender entry can secure the justification of its restriction only if it is harmoniously adjusted in a direction that recognizes the dignity of the transsexual person to the fullest extent even in relation to minor children.
However, according to the Second En Banc Decision, a court dealing with a case of correction of the gender entry by a transsexual person with minor children must refuse permission for correction of the gender entry merely because the person has minor children, without conducting a concrete hearing as to what constitutes the welfare of the minor children, what kind of infringement of welfare may occur depending on the parent’s correction of the gender entry, or whether that infringement is serious and clear. Even in cases where the relevant minor children accept the transsexual father or mother as having the transitioned sex and live stably according to that status while hoping that the father’s or mother’s gender entry in the Family Relations Register will be corrected to reflect reality, the court has no choice but to deny it. This conclusion creates a contradictory situation in which the court, which must protect the rights of transsexual persons and minor children and ensure their peaceful lives, infringes both their rights and destabilizes them.
D. The dissenting opinion says that the First En Banc Decision presented as a basic principle that, in order to permit correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, it must not cause a significant change in the status relationship with others or have a negative impact on society, and that the Second En Banc Decision did not newly establish the fact that a transsexual person has minor children as an independent negative requirement for permission to correct the gender entry, but merely clarified the purport of the First En Banc Decision. However, this interpretation by the dissenting opinion unjustly narrows the significance of the First En Banc Decision in order to maintain the Second En Banc Decision denying correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children.
The First En Banc Decision declared as a principle that, in determining sex, biological factors and mental and social factors must be comprehensively considered, and accordingly, if a person can be recognized as having the transitioned sex, then a transsexual person must be permitted correction of the gender entry in the official record because, unlike at birth, the transitioned sex is to be legally evaluated as that person’s sex. Also, contrary to the dissenting opinion’s assertion, the First En Banc Decision announced that the effect of a decision granting permission for correction of the gender entry or the correction of the sex entry based thereon does not affect the existing status relationship and rights and obligations. In the supplementary opinion to the majority opinion, it was also made clear that it should be understood not as establishing a negative requirement that the transsexual person must not cause a change in the status relationship with others or a negative impact on society, but rather that if the transsexual person is confirmed to be a transsexual person in the true sense, and furthermore if correction of the gender entry is made accordingly, the effect may be permitted as long as it does not retroactively have a significant effect on existing status relationships and the effect is limited to a restricted scope.
E. The dissenting opinion says that because the Constitution and our legal system, including the Civil Act, clearly presuppose that a father is male and a mother is female, granting permission for correction of the gender entry to a transsexual person who has children would create a parent-child relationship not permitted under our legal system and thus cannot be allowed.
However, it cannot be said that a transsexual parent’s correction of the gender entry creates a parent-child relationship or new status relationship not permitted under our legal system. The fact that a parent is a transsexual person does not mean that the person is no longer the child’s biological parent or that the child is not the transsexual person’s biological child. A transsexual person and his or her child retain their unique rights and duties as parent and child regardless of whether it is before or after the transition. The fact that there is no appropriate term other than father or mother to refer to a transitioned parent does not mean that the original rights and duties or status relationship they had as parent and child disappear, cease, or become void. This was already declared in the First En Banc Decision.
F. Article 36(1) of the Constitution provides: 'Marriage and family life shall be founded and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and the equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this.' The dissenting opinion, using the expression 'equality of the sexes' in the above provision, says that our Constitution presupposes that marriage and the family system are founded and maintained on the basis of the distinction between the sexes and the union between differentiated sexes, and that the correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person who has children is not permitted by our Constitution and laws, but that the Second En Banc Decision, although not legally consistent, distinguished between cases where the transsexual person has adult children and cases where the person has minor children by weighing the systematic conformity of our legal system and legal stability against the need for correction of the gender entry, and accordingly treated the permissibility of correction of the gender entry differently.
First, it must be pointed out that the dissenting opinion unjustly interprets the meaning of the Second En Banc Decision regarding correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with children. In the Second En Banc Decision, the Supreme Court did not expressly state the view that, in the case of a transsexual person with minor children, because our Constitution presupposes the distinction between the sexes in the marriage and family system, correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with children is not permitted under our Constitution and laws, or that correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with children causes a change in the children’s status relationship or rights and obligations. Rather, the Second En Banc Decision reaffirmed and declared the legal principle of the First En Banc Decision, which held that the permission for correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register for a transsexual person is a decision intended to confirm the current true sex newly legally evaluated according to transsexuality, and therefore the effect of a decision granting correction or the correction of the sex entry in the Family Relations Register based thereon does not affect the existing status relationship and rights and obligations. It only held that, in the case of minor children, in light of the significant negative impact of a parent’s correction of the gender entry on the welfare of the minor children due to social discrimination and prejudice, the parental duty to protect the minor children from such negative impact, and other circumstances, correction of the gender entry is not permitted when the transsexual person has minor children.
If Article 36(1) of the Constitution is interpreted as the dissenting opinion does, it leads to results not harmonious with the provisions of Article 10, Article 11(1), and Article 37(1) of the Constitution. With respect to the protection of the family community, together with Article 36(1), one must apply the Preamble to Article 10 of the Constitution, which guarantees human dignity and value and the right to pursue happiness, the latter sentence of Article 10 of the Constitution, which states that 'the State shall have the duty to confirm and guarantee the inviolable fundamental human rights of individuals,' Article 11(1), which guarantees the right to equality, and Article 37(1), which states that 'the freedoms and rights of citizens shall not be disregarded on the ground that they are not enumerated in the Constitution.' Ultimately, the State must equally protect the family community of a transsexual person and his or her children without discrimination, just like any other family community. Furthermore, because Article 36(1) of the Constitution declares that, together with the meaning and preciousness of the family community, they must be based on the ideology of 'gender equality' and individual dignity, and that the State protects and guarantees them, it cannot be used as a basis for excluding them from protection according to the type of family life. Article 36(1) of the Constitution should be interpreted prospectively as including the family community of a transsexual person with minor children as a protected subject.
The importance of the family community cannot be overemphasized, and this is no different in the case of transsexual persons. The bond between a transsexual person and his or her family members must also be socially respected and legally protected without discrimination. If transsexual persons and their family members cherish the family community they have formed and wish to continue living while maintaining that bond, the State and society have the duty to respect such wishes to the fullest extent and guarantee their family life. In the case of modern family communities, including the family community of transsexual persons, which are appearing in diverse forms, actively accepting and protecting them within the existing family order to the extent that they do not violate social order and the public welfare strengthens the diversity and soundness of our society and reinforces the safety net surrounding society, thereby promoting the ultimate welfare of members of society.
G. In our society, transsexual persons still must endure, in daily life and legally, the environment of discrimination and exclusion, the division of the self, and the threat to existence, and suffer the pain of not being able to fully complete their narrative in accordance with their actual gender identity. Because of their appearance or mannerisms, transsexual persons are easily exposed to various forms of danger, including sexual violence, and this increases even more when the sex they personally disclose does not match the legal sex indicated in official certificates or documents such as identity cards and passports.
However noble the light of the constitutional spirit that guarantees human dignity and value may be, if that light does not shine equally on members of society, including transsexual minorities, its meaning will fade. Institutional foundations must be laid so that transsexual persons may seek their life according to their true gender identity, and efforts must be made to improve the culture of discrimination that persists in reality. Through this, the constitutional guarantees of human dignity and value and the realization of fundamental rights can become substantive, not merely slogans.
The First En Banc Decision was the fruit of such efforts. The Supreme Court, empathizing with the hardships transsexual persons must endure as a minority, declared that they, as equal members of our society, have the right to request correction of the gender entry in accordance with their gender identity as an extension of human dignity and value and the right to pursue happiness. Correction of the gender entry for transsexual persons does not solve all problems, but it is an important starting point for solving them. Starting from this, in order to truly solve their difficulties and remedy violations of fundamental rights, the voices of transsexual persons and their families must be institutionally reflected through legislation. Since the First En Banc Decision, for 16 years, the establishment of a legal system for transsexual persons has been delayed, and transsexual persons who must still remain in the shadow of exclusion are urgently calling for the guarantee of equal rights. There is a need to listen to the voices of transsexual persons, which resound breaking the icy silence created by the established rigid order, and to adopt an attitude of empathy for their suffering. While emphasizing once again the importance of the judiciary’s role in protecting the rights of transsexual persons, a minority in our society, and the urgency of legislative measures concerning correction of the gender entry, I state this supplementary opinion to the majority opinion."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding the 주관적 범죄성립요건 is correct? (다툼이 있는 경우, according to case law)
A: With the 살의 to kill, if the actor assaults the victim (act (a)), and when the victim loses consciousness and goes limp, mistakenly believes the victim to be dead and buries the victim in sand for the purpose of 증거인멸 (act (b)), and it is found that the victim died from act (b), since the 직접 원인 of death is act (b), attempted murder is established.
B: In order for an actor’s conduct to qualify as 긴급피난, it is sufficient that the actor has only 긴급피난상황에 대한 인식; an intent to avoid the 위험 is not also required.
C: Where a person, with the 목적 of harming another, instigates a person who does not have the 목적 of harming another to commit 위증, under the 공범종속성 principle, the offense of 위증교사, rather than 모해위증교사, is established.
D: If a witness, being 착오, testifies to content contrary to objective facts without awareness that it is contrary to his or her own 기억, intent to commit 위증 can be recognized.
E: Where an actor who accidentally received a 착오송금 from a 거래회사 that is in litigation over a claim for payment of the 물품대금 refuses to return the mistakenly remitted money with the intent to exercise a lawful right of 상계 against the 물품대금, the establishment of the 불법영득의사, which is an element of 횡령죄, may be denied.
